title: The Rochester Cornea Surgeon Who Gave Up His Savings for Hyderabad
dek: In late 1981 Gullapalli Rao and his wife decided to leave a promising American career; six years later their eye institute saw its first patients.

story.event: Leaving a University of Rochester career to found a not-for-profit eye institute in Hyderabad
story.summary: In late 1981 the corneal surgeon Gullapalli N. Rao and his wife Pratibha decided to leave his career at the University of Rochester to build a not-for-profit eye institute in Hyderabad. They gave their savings, raised money through a society in Rochester and, in 1985, secured one crore rupees and five acres in Banjara Hills from the family of the film-maker L. V. Prasad; clinical services began on 1 June 1987. Rao ran it on strict rules, including never relying on grants or donations for running costs, and treated patients whether or not they could pay.
paragraphs: In late 1981, by his own account, Gullapalli Nageswara Rao and his wife Pratibha decided to go home to India. He was a corneal surgeon at the University of Rochester in New York, with dozens of research papers to his name and, a colleague's 2022 profile records, a full professorship within reach. On visits to the All India Ophthalmological Society's annual meetings, he had kept meeting young eye doctors and patients with corneal disease, and had come to see how much greater the need was there.

The profile says it was not an easy decision. He did not want a job in an existing hospital; he wanted a not-for-profit institute in Hyderabad that would combine patient care, teaching and research, and treat every patient to the same standard whatever they could pay. "We donated all our savings and then approached friends and ophthalmic corporations for support," he told Forbes India in 2012. In 1984 the couple set up an Indo-American Eye Care Society in Rochester to raise money, and the chief minister of Andhra Pradesh, N. T. Rama Rao, allotted land at Kismathpur on the city's edge.

The turn came in the summer of 1985, when a mutual friend introduced Rao to Ramesh Prasad, son of the film-maker L. V. Prasad. After going through the proposal, the Prasads gave one crore rupees and five acres in Banjara Hills; the Times of India later traced the money to the profits of the 1981 hit Ek Duuje Ke Liye. The institute took L. V. Prasad's name. Rao stayed on the Rochester faculty until 1986, and the couple's savings went into the first surgical equipment. Clinical services began on 1 June 1987.

The early years were hard. Trained staff were scarce, Rao later said, so the institute built its own training, and some of its methods were "alien to the country", which brought resistance and misunderstanding. He kept the finances deliberately plain: no loans or overdrafts, salaries paid on the last day of each month, and grants and donations never used to meet running costs. By 2012, Forbes India reported, half its patients paid nothing, however complex their treatment.

quote.text: A man ought warily to begin charges which once begun will continue; but in matters that return not, he may be more magnificent.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon separates costs that recur from those that come once. Rao drew the same line: a film family's gift could buy land and buildings, but salaries and daily care had to be paid from what the institute earned, so that free treatment never depended on the next donation.

reflection: Rao's decision is usually told as a sacrifice, and it was one. But the part that kept the institute alive was less dramatic: a clear sense of which costs come round every month, and a refusal to pay those with money that might not come again.

You may have a commitment that began as a one-off and has quietly become a monthly charge on your time or energy. Bacon would say be generous with the one-offs and careful with what repeats. That applies to evenings and weekends as much as to money, and to the people at home who share them.
invitation: List the commitments that come round every week for you, whether money, time or care. Pick one you started without much thought, and decide today whether it has earned its place.

research_notes: Dates of the return disagree. Rao told Forbes India (2012) that he and his wife decided in late 1981 to return; the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology profile (2022) dates the decision to 1982; LVPEI's own profile says he stayed on the Rochester faculty until 1986; The Better India (2020) says they returned in 1981 and launched in 1985, and The Global Indian (2023) says he had returned 'by 1980'. The story follows Rao's own 'late 1981' for the decision and LVPEI's 1986 for leaving Rochester, and does not repeat the 1980 or 1981 return dates. The Prasad gift: Rao (Forbes India), The Global Indian and The Times of India give one crore rupees and five acres; The Better India gives five crore and is not used. Who gave it: Rao names Ramesh Prasad, the Times of India names L. V. Prasad; the story says 'the Prasads'. Savings: Rao says they 'donated all our savings'; the IJO profile says their life savings bought the first equipment; the story uses both, which are compatible. The IJO profile is by Pravin K. Vaddavalli, a director at LVPEI, so it is not independent of the institute; its claims about the decision (the full professorship, the AIOS meetings, 'not an easy decision') are attributed to 'a colleague's 2022 profile'. The Kismathpur land, per Rao, was used for the public health and optometric education division rather than the main hospital. Half of patients paying nothing is Bagchi's 2012 summary in Forbes India. Bacon wrote in English, so no translator; the essay is numbered XXVIII in the standard 1625 order.
